segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Welcome the one who is weak in faith, but not in order to pass judgment on opinions.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: One person believes he may eat anything, but the one who is weak eats vegetables.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The one who eats must not look down on the one who does not eat, and the one who does not eat must not judge the one who eats, for God has welcomed him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Who are you to judge someone else’s household slave? Before his own master he stands or falls. And he will stand, for the Lord is able to make him stand.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: One person judges one day above another; another judges every day alike. Let each be fully convinced in his own mind.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The one who observes the day observes it for the Lord. And the one who eats, eats for the Lord, for he gives thanks to God; and the one who does not eat, it is for the Lord that he does not eat, and he gives thanks to God.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For none of us lives for himself, and none dies for himself.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: If we live, we live for the Lord, and if we die, we die for the Lord. So whether we live or die, we belong to the Lord.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For this is why Christ died and came to life: so that he might be Lord of both the dead and the living.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But you, why do you judge your brother? Or you, why do you look down on your brother? For we will all stand before the judgment seat of God,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: for it is written:

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “As I live, says the Lord, every knee will bow to me, and every tongue will acknowledge God.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So then, each of us will give an account of himself.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So let us no longer judge one another. Instead, let this be your judgment: never to put a stumbling block or a trap in a brother’s way.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: I know and am convinced in the Lord Jesus that nothing is unclean in itself; only to the one who considers something unclean, to that person it is unclean.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For if your brother is distressed because of food, you are no longer walking in love. Do not by your food destroy that person for whom Christ died.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So do not let this good of yours be slandered.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For the kingdom of God is not eating and drinking, but righteousness and peace and joy in the Holy Spirit.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Whoever serves Christ in this way is pleasing to God and approved by people.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So then, let us pursue what makes for peace and for building one another up.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Do not tear down the work of God for the sake of food. All things are clean, but it is bad for the person whose eating is a stumbling block.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: It is good not to eat meat or drink wine or do anything by which your brother stumbles or is made to fall or is weak.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The faith that you have, keep to yourself before God. Blessed is the one who does not judge himself in what he approves.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But the one who has doubts is condemned if he eats, because it is not from faith; and everything that is not from faith is sin.

notes.phrase: not in order to pass judgment on opinions
notes.traditional: not to quarrel over opinions; not to doubtful disputations
notes.note: The Greek phrase is compressed and can be read two ways. Many translations take it as 'not for quarrels over opinions'. The noun elsewhere in the New Testament means distinguishing or assessing, so it is rendered here as passing judgment, which also fits the chapter's repeated warnings against judging. The 'opinions' are the scruples or reasonings of the weak person.

The word denotes a domestic slave, a member of a household who answered to its master alone. Most translations have 'servant', which hides the point that an outsider had no standing to assess another owner's slave. 'Master' and 'the Lord' in this verse translate the same Greek word, and Paul plays on it: the slave's master turns out to be the Lord.

notes.traditional: esteems / regards / considers one day above another
notes.note: The verb is the same one translated 'judge' throughout the chapter, here in its neutral sense of forming an assessment. Most translations vary the English to 'esteems' or 'considers'. 'Judges' is kept so that the reader can hear Paul's repetition of the word. The days in view are probably sabbaths and festivals of the Jewish calendar, though Paul does not say so.

Believers addressed and referred to one another as siblings, and the word here means any fellow member of the community, man or woman. The singular 'brother' is kept throughout the chapter because Paul is picturing one individual facing another.

notes.traditional: the judgment seat of Christ (KJV); the judgment seat of God
notes.note: The word denotes the raised platform from which a magistrate heard cases, a familiar sight in any Roman city. The earliest manuscripts read 'of God'. Many later ones read 'of Christ', probably under the influence of 2 Corinthians 5:10.

With this construction the verb in the Septuagint usually means to give open praise or acknowledgement, and it is so taken here. 'Confess to God' in the sense of admitting sins is possible and would suit the context of judgment. The quotation is Isaiah 45:23, introduced with the oath formula 'As I live, says the Lord', which occurs elsewhere in the prophets.

notes.phrase: will give an account of himself
notes.traditional: will give an account of himself to God
notes.note: Many manuscripts add 'to God' at the end of the verse, and most English translations include it. The SBLGNT text follows the witnesses that lack the words. The sense is the same either way, since the previous verses have already named God as judge.

In the Septuagint and in period usage the word refers to a snare or something that trips a person up, and figuratively to whatever leads someone into ruin or sin. The traditional 'hindrance' is too mild. The related verb in verse 21 is rendered 'is made to fall'.

The Greek word ordinarily means 'common' or 'shared'. In Jewish usage it had come to mean ritually profane, unfit for those keeping the purity and food laws. That usage would have been clear to readers familiar with Jewish practice and puzzling to others. The issue in this chapter is food regarded as defiling, whether under the Mosaic food laws or through other scruples.

notes.traditional: your good; what you regard as good
notes.note: Paul does not say what 'your good' is. Most interpreters take it as the freedom of the strong to eat anything, which would be spoken of as evil if it harmed others. Others take it as the good that the whole community shares, the gospel or its salvation, brought into disrepute among outsiders by the quarrel.

notes.phrase: whose eating is a stumbling block
notes.traditional: who makes another stumble by what he eats; who eats with offence
notes.note: The Greek says literally 'who eats through a stumbling block'. It may refer to the strong person whose eating causes someone else to stumble, which is the more common view and fits verse 21. It may instead refer to the weak person who eats against his conscience and so stumbles. The rendering leaves both possibilities open.

notes.phrase: or is made to fall or is weak
notes.traditional: stumbles (shorter text); stumbleth, or is offended, or is made weak (KJV)
notes.note: Several early and important manuscripts end the verse at 'stumbles', and many modern translations follow them. The SBLGNT prints the longer reading, found in other early witnesses and in the majority of manuscripts, and it is translated here.

The standard view, followed here, is that this form of the verb means to be divided in oneself, to waver or doubt. That sense is not clearly attested before the New Testament, where the form otherwise means to dispute or to make distinctions. A minority of scholars therefore read 'the one who disputes' or 'who makes distinctions'. The verb belongs to the same word-family as 'judge' and 'condemned' in verses 22 and 23, a play on words that English cannot reproduce.

candidates.reason: Used across the letters for fellow believers of either sex; translators split between 'brother', 'brother or sister' and 'fellow believer', and the choice should be uniform.
With its verb σκανδαλίζω it recurs throughout the Gospels and letters and is variously rendered 'stumbling block', 'offence', 'hindrance' or 'cause to sin'; needs one policy.
The middle voice is traditionally 'doubt' (Romans 4:20; James 1:6; Mark 11:23) but the sense is disputed lexically, and the passages should be handled consistently.
In the ritual sense (Mark 7, Acts 10–11, here) it stands beside ἀκάθαρτος; a decision is needed on whether to distinguish 'common/defiled' from 'unclean'.
Recurs in Luke, Acts and Paul, where 'despise' is traditional but now suggests hatred instead of contemptuous dismissal; renderings vary widely.
